summary.text: In 2020 ground tests, the ISS scatter detector's response per unit smoke mass varied more across aerosol types than the other instruments (coefficient of variation 35%, versus 13% for a newer prototype).

technical_detail.text: Wang et al. (2020), p. 9: slopes of detector signal versus PM2.5 mass for reference and smoke aerosols; the authors attribute the ISS detector spread to its differing optics and plumbing. The ISS detector also saturated at higher concentrations.

Derived descriptive fraction 4/15 over 15 primary runs in 15 conservative sample groups (campaigns SAME, SAME-R); airflow 0.0-8.1 cm/s, heater resistance ratio 1.44-1.4524143054229013, heating 60.0-60.0 s, programmed aging 11.0-720.0 s, mixing 8.0-8.0 s; measured ISS scatter 0.001-5.042 V. The 2.0 V label is a derived threshold (Meyer et al. 2018 Figure 9), not a recorded operational alarm, and the fraction is not an alarm probability.

Runs SAME-R:56, SAME-R:58, SAME-R:79, SAME-R:89: airflow 8.1 cm/s, heater resistance ratio 1.445, heating 60.0 s, aging 11.0 s, mixing 8.0 s, microgravity (ISS). These are the runs averaged in the 2012 Table 1 particle-size row. Measured voltages; the 2.0 V comparison level is a derived threshold, not an alarm record.

SAME final report (2010), detector signal traces: flow design range 2-8 cm/s, about 60 s heating below ignition, aging 10-1800 s, microgravity in the MSG. Signals digitised at 1 Hz with an 8-bit converter.
SAME final report (2010), Table 1 discussion (moment-method diameters, baseline unaged vs 720 s aged). Kapton and Teflon smokes had narrow size distributions with little mass above 1 um (Table 1).

catalog_records.material: Lampwick, Kapton, Nomex, Teflon, PMMA, wire insulation
catalog_records.detector: ISS scatter detector, STS ionization detector, CSP prototype, commercial detectors
catalog_records.statement: A 2020 ground study tested whether laboratory reference aerosols can serve as transfer standards for spacecraft smoke-detector testing, using smoke from six spacecraft-relevant materials.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Wang et al. (2020, NTRS 20205003817): mineral oil and DOS reference aerosols together spanned the detector-response range of the six smokes in a mixed chamber at 1 g; smoke size distributions were not measured during the smoke tests.
catalog_records.source_title: Spacecraft Smoke Detector Characterization with Reference and Smoke Aerosols
limitations: Ground (1 g) tests; no alarm evaluation; no microgravity.

catalog_records.material: Lampwick, Kapton, Nomex, Teflon, PMMA, wire insulation
catalog_records.value_unit: % coefficient of variation of response slope across aerosols
catalog_records.statement: In 2020 ground tests, the ISS scatter detector's response per unit smoke mass varied more across aerosol types than the other instruments (coefficient of variation 35%, versus 13% for a newer prototype).
catalog_records.technical_detail: Wang et al. (2020), p. 9: slopes of detector signal versus PM2.5 mass for reference and smoke aerosols; the authors attribute the ISS detector spread to its differing optics and plumbing. The ISS detector also saturated at higher concentrations.
catalog_records.source_title: Spacecraft Smoke Detector Characterization with Reference and Smoke Aerosols
limitations: 1 g ground chamber; response slope, not alarm decisions.

catalog_records.statement: The 2020 ground study included a single PMMA pyrolysis test, so the ISS scatter detector has been exposed to PMMA smoke only once, at 1 g, without an alarm evaluation.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Wang et al. (2020), p. 4: tube-furnace oxidative pyrolysis of lamp wick, Kapton, Nomex, Teflon, PMMA and wire insulation; one PMMA test with 2 g of sample.
catalog_records.source_title: Spacecraft Smoke Detector Characterization with Reference and Smoke Aerosols
catalog_records.source_location: PDF p. 4, Sec. II.C Smoke Aerosol Materials (continues p.5)
limitations: Single 1 g test; detector signal vs mass only.

catalog_records.detector: ISS smoke detector (near-infrared forward light scattering)
catalog_records.value_unit: share of Teflon flight tests without alarm (no denominator published)
catalog_records.statement: In the same ISS experiments, the ISS smoke detector would not have alarmed for about two thirds of the Teflon smoke tests.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Meyer et al. (2018), Section 3.2 and Figure 9; same conditions as the Kapton result (microgravity, MSG, about 60 s pyrolysis heating, 8.1 cm/s baseline flow). Teflon smoke is mostly sub-micron, where forward light scattering is weak. No denominators are published; O2 and pressure are not stated.
catalog_records.source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment
limitations: Applies only to the SAME flight runs analysed in Meyer et al. 2018.
'About two thirds' is the authors' wording; no denominator published.
Not an ISS fire-incident statistic.

catalog_records.statement: The older Space Shuttle ionization detector also stayed below its alarm boundary in some Kapton, Teflon and lamp wick smoke runs.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Meyer et al. (2018), Section 3.2 / Figure 9. The Shuttle detector was run only intermittently (its internal pump drew aerosol at three liters per minute, which ruled out aging tests), so its data set is much smaller than the ISS detector's. Overall it was somewhat less sensitive than the ISS detector but did better on Teflon smoke.
catalog_records.source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment
limitations: Small, intermittent data set for this detector.
No run counts published.
Contrasts with the 2010 SAME report statement that all SAME tests gave strong Shuttle-detector signals (see SAME-EV-002).

catalog_records.detector: ISS smoke detector and Space Shuttle smoke detector
catalog_records.statement: Neither of the two spacecraft smoke detectors flown in the ISS experiment detected every type of smoke produced by overheating common spacecraft materials.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Headline result of Meyer et al. (2018), abstract; based on the SAME flight runs with smoke from five spacecraft materials (Kapton, Teflon, cotton lamp wick, silicone rubber, Pyrell foam) generated by non-flaming pyrolysis in microgravity.
catalog_records.source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment
limitations: Pyrolysis (pre-fire overheat) smoke only; no flaming fires.
Five materials only.
Detector performance judged against threshold lines in Figure 9, not recorded alarms.

catalog_records.statement: Some size discrimination is needed so that a detector can alarm on the weak signal of small Teflon or Kapton smoke without excessive nuisance alarms from large dust particles.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Meyer et al. (2018), Section 3.1, citing Urban et al.; a design need inferred from the measured smoke sizes, not a measured false-alarm result.
catalog_records.source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment
limitations: Nuisance-alarm behaviour argued, not measured, in this paper.

catalog_records.value_unit: ratio of diameter of average mass, zero flow vs 8.1 cm/s
catalog_records.statement: With no forced airflow in microgravity, smoke particles were on average 1.7 times larger (from 1.3 times for Teflon to 2.8 times for Kapton) than at 8.1 cm/s, a low-gravity effect that normal-gravity detector tests do not reproduce.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Meyer et al. (2018), Section 3.3: eleven zero-flow tests; thermal-expansion flow of 0.5-1.5 cm/s; vapour concentration about eight times higher than at 8.1 cm/s. At 1 g buoyancy would widen the mixing zone, so this condition is unique to low gravity. About two thirds of the smoke escaped into the glovebox in these tests, lowering particle counts.
catalog_records.source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment
catalog_records.source_location: 3.3. TEM Results (Impact of flow on particle morphology)
limitations: Eleven tests; hardware not designed for zero flow.
Size ratio reported differently elsewhere in the SAME-R report (see SAMER-EV-002).

catalog_records.statement: NIST's 2018 news release quotes the NASA lead author: the ISS detector easily sensed the large cellulose, silicone and Pyrell smoke particles but often failed on the smaller Teflon and Kapton particles.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Press-release coverage of the 2018 paper (secondary source); the primary result comes from the paper itself.
catalog_records.source_title: NIST/NASA Study Shows One Detector Doesn't 'Fit All' for Smoke in Spacecraft (NIST news release)
catalog_records.source_location: Body, quote from M. Meyer (NASA GRC)
limitations: Secondary source (news release).

catalog_records.detector: ISS smoke detector (light scattering) vs Space Shuttle smoke detector (ionization)
catalog_records.statement: In a typical SAME Teflon run, the Shuttle ionization detector gave a strong signal while the ISS light-scattering detector signal was erratic, because Teflon smoke is mostly smaller than 1 um.
catalog_records.technical_detail: SAME final report (2010), detector signal traces: flow design range 2-8 cm/s, about 60 s heating below ignition, aging 10-1800 s, microgravity in the MSG. Signals digitised at 1 Hz with an 8-bit converter.

catalog_records.statement: The 2010 SAME report says all SAME tests gave strong Space Shuttle ionization-detector signals, whereas the 2018 paper reports some Shuttle-detector runs below the alarm boundary.
catalog_records.technical_detail: SAME final report (2010) versus Meyer et al. (2018), Section 3.2. The two statements describe different test sets and use different criteria, so they are kept as conflicting evidence rather than merged.
catalog_records.source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) - Final Report (Nov 1, 2000 - Apr 14, 2009), dated March 15, 2010, with appended papers (Appendices B-E)
limitations: Different campaigns and criteria; cause of the difference unresolved.

catalog_records.statement: SAME measured small particle sizes for Kapton and Teflon smoke, which makes them hard for light-scattering detectors to sense, while large lamp wick and silicone particles give very large scattering signals.
catalog_records.technical_detail: SAME final report (2010), Table 1 discussion (moment-method diameters, baseline unaged vs 720 s aged). Kapton and Teflon smokes had narrow size distributions with little mass above 1 um (Table 1).
catalog_records.source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) - Final Report (Nov 1, 2000 - Apr 14, 2009), dated March 15, 2010, with appended papers (Appendices B-E)
limitations: Moment-method sizes rely on a lognormal assumption that holds well for Kapton and lamp wick only.

catalog_records.statement: SAME-R states a design trade-off: a scattering detector with enough gain to alarm on weak small-particle Teflon or Kapton smoke risks excessive nuisance alarms from large dust.
catalog_records.source_title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) - Final Report, June 2, 2014 (with Appendices A-F)
catalog_records.source_location: PDF p. 5, A. Moment Instrument Results (p.5)
limitations: Design trade-off; nuisance-alarm rate not measured.

catalog_records.statement: In the 2012 SAME-2 particle-size table, the unaged Teflon row is internally inconsistent: its printed geometric mean and spread imply larger count-mean and mass diameters than the printed ones.
catalog_records.technical_detail: Urban et al. 2012 (AIAA 2012-3536, NTRS 20130000422), Table 1, PDF p. 7: printed 0.081 um geometric mean, 2.198 geometric SD, 0.101 um count mean, 0.17 um mass diameter; recomputed 0.110 and 0.205 um. Nine other rows agree within rounding. The row averages four SAME-R baseline runs.
catalog_records.source_title: Particle Morphology and Size Results from the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-2
catalog_records.source_location: Urban et al. 2012 (AIAA 2012-3536, NTRS 20130000422), Table 1, PDF p. 7
limitations: Source-table inconsistency; it does not affect the detector-response records.

catalog_records.technical_detail: Fortenberry et al. (2021), p. 2, citing SAME papers (refs. 3-5); the authors call this troubling because Kapton and Teflon are abundant in spacecraft electrical systems, where a fire is likely to begin.

detection_blindspots.topic: Heritage spacecraft smoke detectors exposed to flaming-fire smoke in microgravity
detection_blindspots.rule: no microgravity detector test with flaming-fire smoke for the ISS or Shuttle smoke detector

related_tests_other_detectors.detector: commercial ionization sensor + DustTrak DRX with assumed 2 mg/m3 alarm point

detection_blindspots.statement: Within the examined sources, the ISS and Shuttle smoke detectors were evaluated in microgravity only with pre-fire (pyrolysis) smoke, never with smoke from flaming fires; Saffire IV-VI measured flaming-fire smoke with a commercial ionization sensor and an aerosol monitor instead.
detection_blindspots.detail: SAME and SAME-R heated samples below ignition to emulate an overheat event. Saffire IV-VI fires were large flaming burns in an uncrewed Cygnus.

detection_blindspots.topic: ISS smoke-detector response to PMMA smoke
detection_blindspots.rule: material/detector pair not tested in microgravity with an alarm evaluation
detection_blindspots.statement: Within the examined sources, the ISS smoke detector was never tested with PMMA smoke in microgravity and no alarm decision was evaluated for PMMA smoke; its only exposure was a single 1 g ground test that measured signal against smoke mass.
detection_blindspots.detail: Saffire IV-VI burned PMMA in microgravity but measured smoke with a commercial ionization sensor and an aerosol monitor, not with the ISS detector. Model A (BASS-II PMMA flame spread) says nothing about smoke-detector response.

detection_blindspots.topic: Kapton and Teflon detector response differs between SAME (2007) and SAME-R (2010)
detection_blindspots.statement: Within the examined sources, the ISS detector's response to Kapton and Teflon smoke differs strongly between the 2007 SAME and 2010 SAME-R campaigns, and no source explains why.
detection_blindspots.detail: Kapton reached 2.0 V in every SAME run but in a minority of SAME-R runs, while Teflon went the other way; the measured counts are in the cited records.

detection_blindspots.topic: Shuttle detector: 'strong signal in all tests' vs 'some runs below alarm boundary'
detection_blindspots.statement: Within the examined sources, the 2010 SAME report and the 2018 paper disagree on whether the Space Shuttle ionization detector responded to all SAME smokes; the difference may come from test sets and criteria and is unresolved.

detection_blindspots.topic: Size increase of zero-flow smoke reported with different magnitudes
detection_blindspots.statement: Within the examined sources, the zero-flow particle-size increase is reported as 30 % to 40 %, as 2 to 3 times and as 1.7 times on average; the direction agrees but the magnitude is unresolved.

limitations: Results describe the cited experiments and documents only; they are not ISS fire-incident statistics or general detector failure rates.
